summary: Etidronate disodium is a first-generation non-nitrogenous bisphosphonate that inhibits bone resorption and also, at higher doses, mineralization. It is used to treat symptomatic Paget disease of bone and to prevent and treat heterotopic ossification after total hip replacement or spinal cord injury. Doses must be taken on an empty stomach away from food, calcium and antacids, and high-dose or prolonged courses risk a mineralization defect (osteomalacia).
indications: Symptomatic Paget disease of bone (osteitis deformans)
Prevention and treatment of heterotopic ossification following total hip replacement or due to spinal cord injury

dosage.d: 5 mg/kg/day for up to 6 months, or 11-20 mg/kg/day for up to 3 months
dosage.n: Doses above 10 mg/kg/day reserved for special cases; do not exceed 20 mg/kg/day

dosage.d: 20 mg/kg/day for 1 month before and 3 months after surgery (4 months total)
20 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks, then 10 mg/kg/day for 10 weeks (12 weeks total)
dosage.n: Start as soon as feasible after injury

dosage.d: Repeat courses only after a drug-free interval >= 3 months

admin: Take as a single oral dose on an empty stomach with water
Do not take food, milk, calcium, iron, magnesium or aluminum-containing antacids within 2 hours of dosing (they impair absorption)
Maintain adequate dietary calcium and vitamin D, but separate from the dose
For divided dosing due to GI upset, split the daily dose but keep total constant
Stay upright if reflux/esophageal symptoms occur
moa: Etidronate is a pyrophosphate analog that adsorbs to hydroxyapatite crystals in bone. It inhibits osteoclast-mediated bone resorption and reduces abnormally high bone turnover in Paget disease. At higher doses it also inhibits mineralization of newly formed bone, which underlies its use in heterotopic ossification but also the risk of a mineralization defect (osteomalacia) with prolonged high-dose therapy.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to etidronate or other bisphosphonates
relative: Significant renal impairment (avoid in severe; reduce/withhold if SCr rises)
Enterocolitis (use lower end of dose range)
Fractures associated with Paget disease (use lowest effective dose)
monitor: Patients on high-dose or prolonged courses for mineralization defect

preg: Etidronate is pregnancy category C; bisphosphonates accumulate in fetal bone and may cause skeletal effects. Avoid in pregnancy unless the potential benefit justifies the risk.
lact: It is not known whether etidronate is excreted in human milk; because of potential effects on infant bone, avoid use or discontinue nursing.
renal: Use with caution in renal impairment; etidronate is contraindicated/should be avoided in severe renal impairment. Withhold or reduce the dose if serum creatinine rises during therapy and monitor renal function.
hepatic: No specific hepatic dose adjustment is required; etidronate is not significantly metabolized by the liver.

moderate: Calcium, iron, magnesium or aluminum-containing products and antacids - reduce etidronate absorption; separate by >= 2 hours
Warfarin - rare reports of altered prothrombin time; monitor INR
minor: Other drugs causing GI irritation - additive dyspepsia
interactions.food: Food, especially dairy and calcium-rich items, chelates etidronate and reduces absorption - take on an empty stomach 2 hours from meals.
interactions.alcohol: No direct interaction; limit alcohol for bone and gastrointestinal health.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause transient rise in serum phosphate and a mild, reversible increase that can affect bone-turnover markers; can elevate creatinine if renal function declines.

common: Bone pain or increased pain at pagetic sites
serious: Mineralization defect / osteomalacia with high-dose or prolonged use
Increased risk of fracture (non-spinal) in Paget disease at high doses
rare: Osteonecrosis of the jaw (rare, mainly with high-dose/long-term bisphosphonate use)

monitoring: Serum phosphate and calcium during therapy
Renal function (serum creatinine) before and during treatment
Serum alkaline phosphatase and clinical response in Paget disease
Symptoms of bone pain or new fractures; dental status for prolonged therapy
counsel: Take on an empty stomach with water; do not eat, drink milk or take calcium/antacids for 2 hours around the dose
Keep up calcium and vitamin D intake but take them separately from this medicine
Report increasing bone pain or new fractures
Tell your dentist you take a bisphosphonate; report jaw pain or numbness, or new thigh/groin pain
pk: Reduction in bone turnover over weeks (Paget)
Plasma peak ~2 hours; only ~1-6% absorbed orally
Plasma half-life ~6 hours; skeletal retention prolonged (months)
Effect persists after stopping due to bone binding
pearls: Take on an empty stomach away from calcium/dairy/antacids - oral bioavailability is very low and easily reduced
High-dose or prolonged courses risk a mineralization defect (osteomalacia) and fractures - keep courses limited (Paget <= 6 months) with drug-free intervals
Useful for heterotopic ossification prophylaxis after hip replacement or spinal cord injury
Older, weaker bisphosphonate; largely superseded by nitrogenous bisphosphonates for many indications
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as you remember on an empty stomach; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose. Do not take two doses together.
overdose: Overdose may cause hypocalcemia (paresthesia, tetany) and GI upset; large ingestions can affect renal function. Treat with milk or antacids to bind the drug, correct hypocalcemia, and provide supportive care.
